course.title: AI-Assisted Engineering and Code Review
course.description: Work with coding assistants as an engineer who owns the result: instructions and context, specs and tests first, small steps, reading and securing machine-written changes, and measuring the effect.
course.audience: A developer who can read Python and SQL and use git. The ai-engineering and ai-agents courses explain how models and agents work; this one is about using them and reviewing their output.

paragraphs: A coding assistant takes a request written in ordinary language, reads whatever part of a project it has been shown, and returns code, often a whole function within a few seconds. What it returns has the same fluent surface whether it is right or wrong, because the assistant writes what code of that kind usually looks like, and it carries no responsibility once the change is merged. The person who merges it does, which is why working with an assistant remains engineering: deciding what the assistant is shown, stating what a change must do before it is built, and reading what comes back against that statement.

Most of that work can be settled with a careful look at the code and some simple arithmetic. A specification written as statements a test can pass or fail tells you which lines of a diff were asked for, a test log you have read yourself tells you more than a report that all tests pass, and the share of merged changes that later fail tells you whether an assistant has made a team better or only faster. The tools change every few months, so they appear here only as current examples, and the habits of checking their work do not depend on any one of them.
outcomes: You'll be able to write a specification and tests that an assistant's change must satisfy.
You'll be able to read a diff against its intent and find unrequested changes.
You'll be able to spot typical machine-made defects and security faults.
You'll be able to separate an assistant's claim from evidence.
You'll be able to write working rules and measure whether assistance helps.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, Python for Data Analysis, SQL: From Rows to Reports, Git and Version Control, Software Testing and Quality.

concepts.title: Assistant modes
concepts.summary: Inline completion, chat, and agentic editing in which the tool reads files, runs commands and edits.

concepts.title: Accountability
concepts.summary: The person who merges a change owns it, whatever wrote it.

concepts.title: Acceptance rate
concepts.summary: The share of suggested code kept unchanged.

concepts.title: Context
concepts.summary: Everything the model sees on a call: instructions, files, history and tool results.

concepts.title: Instruction file
concepts.summary: A checked-in text file of commands, conventions and boundaries read at the start of each session.

concepts.title: Context pollution
concepts.summary: Stale, irrelevant or contradictory text in the context that degrades output.

concepts.title: Acceptance criteria
concepts.summary: Statements that a test can pass or fail.

concepts.title: Edge case
concepts.summary: Input at a boundary or outside the usual range where behaviour must be stated.

concepts.title: Non-goal
concepts.summary: Something the change must not do.

concepts.title: Assertion
concepts.summary: A check inside a test that fails when behaviour is wrong.

concepts.title: Mutation score
concepts.summary: The share of deliberately injected faults that the tests detect.

concepts.title: Coverage
concepts.summary: The share of lines that run during tests, which says nothing about whether outputs are checked.

concepts.title: Commit
concepts.summary: A recorded, reversible snapshot of a change.

concepts.title: Checkpoint
concepts.summary: A commit made before a risky step so that you can return to it.

concepts.title: Revert
concepts.summary: A new commit that undoes an earlier one without rewriting history.

concepts.title: Entry point
concepts.summary: Where execution starts, such as a main function or a route table.

concepts.title: Module boundary
concepts.summary: The line between parts that other parts reach only through an interface.

concepts.title: Claim check
concepts.summary: Confirming a statement about code by finding the line that makes it true.

concepts.title: Scope creep
concepts.summary: Changes beyond what the specification asked for.

concepts.title: Review order
concepts.summary: Intent and design first, then interfaces, tests, risky paths, then details.

concepts.title: Review comment
concepts.summary: A specific, actionable note tied to a line and a reason.

concepts.title: Hallucinated API
concepts.summary: A call to a function, method or package that does not exist.

concepts.title: Swallowed error
concepts.summary: An exception caught and replaced by a default so the failure disappears.

concepts.title: Off-by-one
concepts.summary: A boundary error of exactly one element.

concepts.title: SQL injection
concepts.summary: Attacker-controlled text altering the structure of a query.

concepts.title: Broken access control
concepts.summary: A request reaching data its caller should not see.

concepts.title: Dependency risk
concepts.summary: Adding a package that is unmaintained, malicious or non-existent in the registry the name was guessed from.

concepts.title: Evidence ladder
concepts.summary: Claim, read code, tests pass, run the feature, check in a realistic environment.

concepts.title: Property

concepts.title: Definition of done
concepts.summary: The evidence you require before merging.

concepts.title: Team policy

concepts.title: Change failure rate
concepts.summary: The share of changes that cause a failure needing a fix.

blocks.text: In 2025 the research group METR gave 16 experienced open-source developers 246 real tasks from repositories they had worked in for years, and assigned each task by chance to be done with AI tools or without them. The developers forecast beforehand that the tools would cut their time by 24%. With the tools allowed, the tasks took 19% *longer*, and even after the study the developers believed they had been 20% faster.
A gap of that size between how a tool feels and what it measurably does is a good reason to be exact about what an assistant is.

steps.headline: Three ways to use an assistant

lead.text: A tool that works by **inline completion** sees the text around your cursor and offers a few lines of continuation, which you accept with a keystroke or ignore. A tool that works by **chat** takes whatever you paste or attach, answers in a reply, and leaves it to you to carry the answer back into the file.

The third kind is the **agentic** assistant. It is given a goal, opens the files it thinks relevant, edits them in your working copy, and runs commands such as a search or the [[test suite|The automated tests of a project, run together. Met in Software Testing and Quality.]] to see whether the edit worked. The figure sets the three side by side, row by row.

afterFigure.text: The rows are ordered by reach. Moving from completion to chat to agent, the tool gains the ability to read more of the project, to alter more of it, and to act without you in between, so the amount of work an assistant does on its own *grows* at the same moment as the amount you did not watch grows.

reveal.text: It is inline completion. The test for the mode is what the tool reads and where its output lands, and here it reads the cursor and writes at the cursor.

lead.text: It is easy to talk to an assistant as though it had been on your team for a year. It has not. Whatever it knows about your project is the text that reached it on this turn: the lines near your cursor, the files you attached, the files an agent chose to open, and the output of commands it ran. A convention that lives only in the head of the senior developer, or in a file the agent never opened, does not exist for it.

This is the first of three places where a mistake enters. The second is **plausible code**: the assistant produces text shaped like a correct solution, and the shape is easy to mistake for correctness. The third is **unverified claims**. An assistant that writes "this fixes the bug" is describing what it intended, and nothing in the sentence shows that the bug is gone.

reveal.text: The agent ran the tests that existed. A report of a run shows which checks did not object, and whether they were the right checks is left open.

lead.text: The 42 tests were written by people who each had some behaviour in mind, and the suite covers those behaviours and nothing else. An agent that runs it has therefore done exactly one thing, which is to show that none of those 42 checks failed. It has not shown that the change does what you asked, because your request may not be among the things anyone thought to check.
For that reason the sentence "the tests pass" is evidence only to the degree that the tests describe the request.

Every project keeps a record of who did what to a change. The author field may name a colleague, a contractor or an assistant, and it changes nothing about who answers when the change breaks production at night: that is the person who merged it, and so the person who is **accountable** for it.

An assistant cannot be asked why it did what it did in a way that has consequences, cannot be woken at night, and does not stay with the project. A reviewer who approves a change has accepted a share of that responsibility, and the one who presses merge accepts the rest.

lead.text: The simplest number teams track is the **acceptance rate**, the lines kept unchanged divided by the lines suggested, written as a percentage. If an assistant suggests 160 lines and you keep 136 of them as they came, the rate is 136 / 160, which is 0.85, or 85%. Lines you edited before keeping do not count as kept unchanged, and neither do lines you deleted.

steps.headline: For 200 suggested lines, with 130 kept unchanged and 50 edited before being kept, work out the acceptance rate and the share not kept unchanged.

workedSteps.text: Only lines kept as they came count, so the 50 edited lines are left out of the top of the fraction.
The bottom of the fraction is everything the assistant suggested, edited or not.
Dividing the kept lines by the suggested lines and scaling to a percentage gives the acceptance rate.
The edited lines and the dropped lines make up the rest of the suggestion.

steps.headline: Now the same method on a different morning: 150 lines suggested, 96 kept unchanged.

workedSteps.text: The top of the fraction is the lines kept unchanged.
The bottom is the lines suggested.
The acceptance rate is the first of these as a share of the second, written as a percentage.

reveal.text: The rate counts what people kept. It cannot tell you whether the kept code was right, and developers may keep more because they review less.

recap.keyIdea: An assistant, whichever mode it works in, only sees what it is given and does not carry the responsibility, so the person who merges its change owns it.

blocks.text: You compared three modes by what they read, change and run, and saw that the reach of an agent is exactly what makes its reports need checking. A passing test run describes the tests, and the acceptance rate describes what you kept, so neither measures whether the code is right.
What the assistant sees decides what it can get right, which is the subject of the next lesson.

lessons.title: Context and instruction files

blocks.text: A codebase of 40,000 lines is about 400,000 tokens of text, the small chunks a model reads text in, at the rough rate of 10 tokens a line, and an assistant with a 200,000-token window can hold half of it at once. Everything the assistant does on a task comes out of what it can see, so the question of what to put in front of it is a real engineering decision, made before the first request.

Part of that decision belongs to each task, since it means choosing the files the change needs. The rest can be written down once, in a file in the repository that the assistant reads at the start of every session, so that the project's commands and conventions never have to be repeated.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate whether a codebase fits in a context window, choose what belongs in an instruction file, and know when to reset a session.
intro.whyItMatters: An assistant given the right small context beats one handed everything.

lead.text: On every call, an assistant receives one block of text, called its **context**. It holds the project instructions, the files you or the agent have added, the whole conversation so far, and the output of every command that has run.

The block has a ceiling, the **context window**, measured in **tokens**, the small chunks of text a model reads. For code, a rough working figure is about 10 tokens a line. Multiply the lines in a codebase by 10 and you have the size it would need, and dividing the window by that gives the share that fits.

afterFigure.text: At 10,000 lines the codebase uses half the window and everything fits. At 40,000 lines it needs twice the window, so only half can be present at once, and at 100,000 lines the window covers a fifth.

reveal.text: Resetting with a summary is the usual remedy. The summary carries over the findings, and the new session starts without the dead ends.

lead.text: It is tempting to read the arithmetic above as a reason to find a bigger window and load everything. The difficulty is that a model gives the same attention to a sentence about a database migration and a sentence about a button colour, so text that has nothing to do with the task does not sit quietly. It competes with the text that matters, and it can pull the answer towards code the task never needed to touch.

A long session produces the same effect from the inside. Each failed attempt, each pasted error and each correction you gave stays in the window, and by the fifth attempt the context contains more dead ends than facts. This build-up of stale, irrelevant or contradicting text is called **context pollution**, and the remedy is the same as for the codebase: put less in, and make sure what is there is what the task needs.

afterFigure.text: A practical rule follows. Give the assistant the files the change will touch, the files that define the interfaces it must respect, and the tests, and leave the rest of the repository for it to ask about.

lead.text: Some of what the assistant needs does not appear in the code. How do you run the tests? Which directory is generated and must not be edited? Which logger does the project use? A person learns these from colleagues, and an assistant learns them only if they are written down where it will look. That place is the **instruction file**, a text file at the root of the repository that is read at the start of every session. Several tools agree on the name `AGENTS.md`, and some also read a file named for themselves.

Because the file is read every time, each line costs space on every task, so the test for a line is whether the assistant would do something different after reading it. "Run pnpm check before reporting done" passes, because it names a command and a moment. "Write clean code" fails, because the assistant already intends to and the line names nothing it could check.

afterFigure.text: The lines that survive are of three kinds: commands to build, test and check, conventions the code follows, and boundaries, meaning actions or directories that are off limits.

lessons.title: Specification first

blocks.text: A one-line request, "write a function `slugify(text)` for article titles", can be satisfied by at least two different functions. Both are reasonable readings of the request, and an assistant will pick one without telling you.

What removes the choice is a short list of statements about the result, each precise enough that a test could pass or fail it, written before any code exists. It takes a few minutes to write, and it decides which `slugify` you get.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write acceptance criteria that a test can pass or fail, list the edge cases and non-goals, and derive a test input from each criterion.
intro.whyItMatters: Whatever you leave unstated, the assistant decides for you.

steps.headline: A request is not a spec

lead.text: Suppose you ask an assistant for a function `slugify(text)` that turns an article title into something safe for a web address. The request sounds complete, yet the figure shows two different functions that both fit it.

On the plain title `"Hello"` the two agree. On `"  Hello, World! "` they return `"--hello,-world!-"` and `"hello-world"`. Neither function is wrong, because nothing in the request said which was wanted. The assistant returns the reading it finds most likely and presents it with the same confidence either way.

afterFigure.text: A longer, more detailed prompt does not close the gap by itself, since detail about *how* to write the code says nothing about what must be true of the result. What closes it is a statement of what is observably true afterwards.

reveal.text: The line that pairs the input with the exact result is the one a test can check. The others leave each reader to decide what counts.

lead.text: A spec is a short list of **acceptance criteria**, each one a statement about the result that a test can pass or fail without anyone interpreting it. For `slugify` they read: the output is lowercase; each run of characters that are not letters or digits becomes one hyphen; there is no hyphen at either end; empty input returns an empty string. Four lines replace the whole difference between the two readings above.

The test of a good criterion is whether you can write down an input and the expected output for it. "Handles titles sensibly" fails that test, because no input can be paired with "sensibly". "`slugify('A  B--C')` returns `'a-b-c'`" passes it, since the input and the result are both written out. The figure pairs each criterion with such a test.

workedSteps.text: Start from the input exactly as written, with two spaces after Top and two hyphens after the 10.
The first criterion makes the output lowercase.
The second criterion turns each run of other characters into one hyphen, and no run touches either end, so the third criterion changes nothing.

steps.headline: Derive the expected output for `slugify('  Release Notes, v2! ')`.

workedSteps.text: Lowercase it. The input begins with two spaces and ends with an exclamation mark and a space.
The space between the first two words is one run, and the comma and space before v2 are another, so each becomes one hyphen. The runs at the start and the end become hyphens as well, for the moment.
The third criterion allows no hyphen at either end.

lead.text: An **edge case** is an input at a boundary or outside the usual range: the empty string, an input with no letters at all, a very long title, a title in another alphabet. The behaviour for these is rarely obvious, and a model that has written many slug functions will have written the main case far more often than the boundary ones.

You should therefore list the edge cases yourself, and give each one an expected result. For `slugify`, the empty string is settled by a criterion of its own, while a title made only of spaces and punctuation is not mentioned anywhere, so its result has to be worked out from the other three criteria before anyone can write a test for it. The next screen asks you to do that.

reveal.text: Nothing is left once the end runs are removed, so the result is the empty string. An answer for this input had to be written down, because the main case gives no hint of it.

lead.text: Acceptance criteria say what must be true afterwards. The other half of a spec says what must stay as it is, and a line of that kind is called a **non-goal**. Typical non-goals for `slugify` are that no new dependency is added, that no other function in the file is changed, and that the stored titles are left alone.

Without them, an assistant that has been asked to make a change is free to make nearby ones too: tidy an unrelated function, add a library because it does the job in one line, rename something for consistency. A short list of non-goals marks the edges of the work, and anything outside them is unrequested.

After the assistant has produced `slugify`, you read its change against the spec, line by line. Does it meet each criterion? Does it handle each listed edge case? Has it stayed inside the non-goals? A change that passes the tests but adds a dependency has failed a non-goal, and a change that returns `"-"` for `"  ...  "` has failed a criterion the tests might never have exercised.
A reviewer who has only the generated code must guess what it was meant to do, and ends up approving whatever it does. A reviewer with the spec has an independent standard to hold it against.

reveal.text: It breaks the criterion that no hyphen may sit at either end. The one-line version makes a run at either end into a hyphen, so the two inputs that begin or end with punctuation or spaces come out wrong.

recap.keyIdea: A specification states what is observably true afterwards as criteria a test can check, adds the edge cases and the non-goals, and then serves as the checklist for review.

blocks.text: You turned a vague request into four criteria, derived the expected output for each by working the rules through the input, and added the empty and punctuation-only inputs that the main case never exercises. The non-goals marked what the change must leave alone.
Criteria that a test can pass or fail are close to tests already.

lessons.title: Tests as the contract

blocks.text: A function that decides whether a year is a leap year can be written in one line, `year % 4 == 0`, and it passes the obvious tests: 2024 is a leap year and 2023 is not. The tests passed because nobody asked the question that would have exposed the mistake.
That gap, between a suite that passes and a suite that would catch a defect, matters more when an assistant writes the code, since the code looks right and the green run makes it feel checked.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say why line coverage cannot show that code is checked, find the input that exposes a weak test, and compute a mutation score.
intro.whyItMatters: A passing suite only helps when it could have failed.

lead.text: Here is a function that decides whether a year is a leap year: `year % 4 == 0`. It passes two tests, one asserting that 2024 is a leap year and one that 2023 is not. Every line of the function runs when the tests run, so a coverage report would say 100%, and a reviewer shown only the green result might reasonably stop.
The function is wrong all the same. The two test years happen to be classified correctly by the shortcut, so the two tests could never have noticed. The next screen asks you to find it.

reveal.text: Century years divisible by 100 but not by 400 are not leap years, so 1900 is the year that exposes the shortcut, while 2000 would pass it.

lead.text: The rule being broken is the century rule: a year divisible by 100 is *not* a leap year unless it is also divisible by 400, so 1900 is not leap and 2000 is. A function that ignores it agrees with the true rule on most years, which is exactly why a few tests can pass.

The tool that reported 100% was measuring [[line coverage|The share of a program's lines that run while the tests run. Met in Software Testing and Quality.]], which counts lines that executed. It cannot see whether anything was compared afterwards. The comparison is made by an **assertion**, a check inside a test that fails when the behaviour is wrong. A test that calls the function and asserts nothing adds to coverage and cannot fail, so a suite can reach 100% line coverage while checking almost nothing.

afterFigure.text: The figure adds the third test. It asserts that 1900 is not a leap year, the function returns True, and the check fails, which no amount of coverage would have revealed.

lead.text: If you want to know whether a suite would catch a defect, you can plant one and see. Change an operator in the code, run the tests, and note whether any fail. Each changed copy of the code is a **mutant**: a mutant the tests catch is said to be **killed**, and one that leaves every test passing has **survived**. The share killed is the **mutation score**, and each survivor is a place where the tests would let a real defect through.

The figure applies five changes to the leap-year function. Three of them break the 2024 or 2023 check and are killed. The other two, using 8 or 2 in place of 4, return the right answer for both test years, so the tests cannot tell them from the original. A surviving mutant tells you what to add: a year where the changed and the original code disagree.

lead.text: It is tempting to let the assistant write the function and then write the tests too. The trouble is that tests written by the same author after the code tend to describe what the code does, so they pass by construction, and a mistaken belief in the code shows up equally in the tests.

The safer order is the one from the last lesson: take the criteria, write a test for each one, and run them before the code is generated, when every one should fail. That failure is evidence that the test can fail at all. An assistant that is only told to "make the tests pass" will sometimes pass them by special-casing the listed inputs, returning the expected answer for 2024 and 2023 and nothing else.

reveal.text: Two years are wrong, 1900 and 2100. A suite that included either would have exposed the shortcut.

recap.keyIdea: A passing suite shows only what its assertions check, so judge a suite by whether it would catch a defect, as a mutation score does, and not by the lines it runs.

blocks.text: You saw that a function wrong for 1900 passed every test and had full line coverage, because coverage counts execution and an assertion is what counts correctness. Injecting faults gave a score for the suite directly, and the survivors pointed at the inputs the tests lacked.
Tests written first, from the spec, are the contract. The next lesson asks how to hold the assistant to that contract in steps small enough to check.

lessons.title: Small steps and version control

blocks.text: An agent can deliver 1,200 changed lines as one change or as four changes of 300, and the code in the two cases may be identical.

Version control is what makes small steps cheap. A commit records a state you can return to, so splitting a task into steps and committing a checkpoint before each risky one lets you decide how large each piece of an agent's work may be.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split a large change into commits of a chosen size, commit a checkpoint before risky work, and choose between revert and reset.
intro.whyItMatters: Small steps make each change reviewable and each mistake reversible.

lead.text: An agent given a broad task can return 1,200 changed lines at once, and the natural thing to do is to read it from the top. By the second hundred lines attention has fallen, and by the fifth the reading has turned into scrolling, so the reviewer approves what looked reasonable at a glance. Google's code review guidance asks authors for small changes for this reason, since reviewers find defects in small changes and miss them in large ones.
As four steps of 300 lines, each piece has its own test and its own commit, so each can be read, run and undone without touching the others.

lead.text: The size limit gives a count, but the cuts should follow the task. A feature usually has seams: a data query, then the formatting of its result, then the endpoint that serves it, then the screen that shows it. A **commit** is a recorded snapshot of a change that can be undone later, and a series of commits that each pass their tests is a history in which every step is a state you could return to.
The boundaries are yours to draw. Say what each step is, ask for it alone, and commit it with a message that states what it does and why.

afterFigure.text: The count of steps is the lines divided by the limit, rounded *up*, since a step cannot be split further and a remainder still needs a commit.

lead.text: Before you let an agent edit across many files, commit the state you have, which is already good. That commit is a **checkpoint**, and it costs nothing. If the agent's edit goes wrong, you have a known state to return to, and you do not have to work out by hand which of forty changed files was the harm.

Git then offers two ways back, and they differ in what they do to history. `git revert` adds a new commit that applies the opposite of an earlier one, so the history keeps both the bad commit and its reversal. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` moves the branch back one commit and leaves that commit's changes staged, so the bad commit disappears from the branch. The figure shows both from the same starting point.

afterFigure.text: A revert is safe on a branch others have pulled, because nothing they hold is removed. A reset rewrites history, which is fine on your own local work and a hazard once someone else has the commit.

lead.text: An agent can run git commands as easily as it edits files, and many will commit as they go if allowed. It is convenient, but the commit boundaries it picks reflect its working order, not the way you would want the change reviewed. A series of commits titled "fix", "fix again" and "final" is a record of a conversation with the assistant, and it gives a reviewer no unit to approve.
Take the boundaries back. Ask for one step at a time, run that step's test, look at the diff, and commit it with a message you have read.

reveal.text: Five commits: A, B, C, D and the revert. The revert is a new commit, so the bad commit and its reversal are both in the history.

lessons.reviewLabel: Recovering your bearings in unfamiliar code

blocks.text: Ask an assistant to describe a small web application and it may tell you that the database is reached only through `db.py` and that every route checks the caller's login. Each statement is specific and easy to believe, and either may be false.
A description of that kind reads like a map, and a reader who cannot tell whether the map is accurate is worse off than one with none, because the map is believed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the entry point of a codebase, check whether a module boundary holds, and confirm or refute an assistant's claim by finding the line that decides it.
intro.whyItMatters: You cannot review a change in code whose structure you have taken on trust.

lead.text: You are handed a repository that an assistant wrote last week, and you ask it for a summary. It may be entirely right. It may also describe the structure a project of this kind usually has, which is not the same as the structure this one has, and nothing in the style of the answer tells the two apart.

File names do not settle it either. A name such as `auth.py` shows what the author meant the file to hold, and the code shows what it does. The way to recover the structure is therefore to read a small number of places in the code itself, and to check the assistant's claims against them.

reveal.text: `main.py` is the likely answer. It creates the application and registers the routes, which is the first step of every request.

lead.text: An **entry point** is where execution starts: a main function, a script run from the command line, or a table of routes that maps each URL to a handler. In a small web application the entry point is usually `main.py`, which creates the application and registers the routes. From there you pick one request, say a `GET` to `/orders`, and follow it: `main.py` hands it to `routes/orders.py`, which asks `db.py` for the rows.
The figure draws that path, along with the file tree and the **import graph**, which shows for a module the other modules that import it.

reveal.text: The other four modules do not import it. Three of seven reach the database directly, which is a fact about the structure that the file tree would never have shown.

lead.text: Suppose the assistant's summary says that database access goes through one module. That statement describes a **module boundary**: the line between a part of the program and the rest, crossed only through a small set of functions. The import graph tests it directly. If the claim held, the database module would be imported by one other module, which would sit in front of it. Three route modules import `db.py` themselves, so the claim does not hold, and each route is free to run its own queries.

Boundaries matter to a reviewer because a change to a module with a clean boundary stays inside it, and a change to one without is likely to reach several others. When you ask an assistant to change `db.py`, you now know that three route modules are affected too.

A handful of places carry most of the structure. The entry point shows the order of execution. The data access shows what the program stores and which modules touch it. The authentication shows who may do what. The error handling shows what the program does when something fails, and the configuration shows what can be changed without editing code. The tests show what the author thought important to check, and which behaviours they left unchecked.

Search is the tool for the cross-cutting ones. A search for the authentication decorator lists every place it is used, so the routes that lack it are visible as the gaps, and a search for the database library lists every module that talks to the database.

steps.headline: The assistant says every route checks auth. A search for the decorator finds it on 4 of 6 routes. Check the claim.

workedSteps.text: State the claim so that it can be searched for: every route carries the decorator.
Search the code for the decorator and count the routes that carry it.
The routes that lack it are the ones the claim missed.
Open one of them and look at its handler, to see whether the check lives somewhere else before calling the claim false.

steps.headline: The assistant says no module outside `config.py` reads environment variables. Check the claim.

workedSteps.text: A search for `os.environ` finds 6 matches: 2 in `config.py`, 3 in `billing.py` and 1 in `mail.py`.
A match in `config.py` is allowed, and a match in any other module breaks the claim.

lead.text: What you have just done is a **claim check**: you took a sentence about the code and looked for the line that makes it true or false. The method is the same each time. Turn the claim into something searchable, run the search, count the places that satisfy it against the places that should, and open one exception to see whether it is real.

Make the checks small and numerical. "Auth is handled" is easy to agree with and impossible to check. "Every route carries the decorator" gives a count, and a count that comes out one short is a finding you can show to someone else.

lessons.title: Reading a diff for intent

blocks.text: A request to give the function `list_orders` an optional limit, with a default of 50, needs two edits: a new parameter in the signature and a `LIMIT` in the SQL. The diff an assistant returns for that request may well contain more, because an assistant working in a file tends to tidy, reorder and remove things as it goes.
Reading a diff well means reading it against the request, so that every changed line either answers to the specification or needs a reason.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tag each change in a diff against its spec, read a review in a fixed order, and write a comment that names the line, the concern and the request.
intro.whyItMatters: Plausible changes that nobody asked for are what a casual read lets through.

lead.text: A diff arrives from an assistant, and the habit is to open it at the first changed line and read downwards. A diff shows what changed, and it says nothing of what *should* have changed, so reading it cold leaves you to guess the intent from the code and to approve whatever the code seems to be trying to do.

Begin instead with the specification from earlier in the course. For `list_orders` the spec says: add an optional limit to the function, default 50. With that in hand each **hunk**, a block of neighbouring changed lines in the diff, can be asked one question, whether the spec asks for it.

reveal.text: Two do: the `ORDER BY` and the deleted log line.

lead.text: The figure tags the four changed lines against the spec. The signature change and the `LIMIT` are what was asked for. The `ORDER BY` was not, and it is more than tidying: it changes the order in which every caller receives its orders, so code that relied on the old order may now behave differently. The deleted log line was not asked for either, and logs and error handling carry operational behaviour, since a team may rely on that line to see how often the function is called.

Changes of this kind are called **scope creep**. Individually they look harmless and often are helpful, which is why they pass; in a large diff they hide in the noise. A line that mixes a requested change with an unrequested one, like the SQL line here, needs to be read twice.

afterFigure.text: A change beyond the spec has two honest outcomes. It is removed from this change, or the author gives a reason for it and the spec is amended to include it.

lead.text: The most expensive faults sit at the top: a change that solves the wrong problem, or solves the right one in the wrong place, cannot be rescued by tidy naming. So read the spec first, then ask whether the design is sensible, then look at the interfaces that the change alters and at who else calls them. After that come the tests.

The last two steps are the risky paths, meaning error handling, logging, authentication and anything touching data, and finally the details such as names and style. Details are last because a diff that fails an earlier step makes them moot, and because tools can check many of them for you.

lead.text: A **review comment** that reads "this looks risky" leaves the author to guess where and why, and a question such as "why did you change this?" gets an answer about the past and no change in the code. A comment that works has three parts: the line it concerns, the concern with its reason, and what you want done.

"Line 12 drops the audit log. Please restore it or explain why it is not needed" has all three. The same form applies when the author is an assistant, since you can paste the comment into the session as the next instruction.

reveal.text: The comment that names the line, states the concern and asks for a specific action gives the author everything needed to respond.

recap.keyIdea: Read a diff against its specification, in order from intent to detail, and treat every change the spec did not ask for as something to remove or justify.

blocks.text: You tagged four changes in a diff against the spec and found two that were not asked for, one of which removed behaviour a team might depend on. Starting from the spec and working down to the details meant the unrequested changes showed up as gaps between the spec and the diff.
The next step is to know what kinds of fault to expect inside the requested changes themselves.

lessons.title: Defects that assistants typically make

blocks.text: A function that returns a page of ten items from a list uses the slice `items[page*size:(page+1)*size]`. It runs, it returns ten items, and a quick test passes. For a caller who counts pages from 1 it is also wrong, because the slice was written for pages counted from 0, and nothing in the code or in its output says which convention is in use.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name four defects that assistants make, trace a slice to find an off-by-one, and spot a swallowed error or a bent test.
intro.whyItMatters: The defects that run are the ones a quick read lets through.

lead.text: A person who writes a bug usually knows the code is unfinished. An assistant produces text shaped like finished code every time, so its faults arrive with the same fluent surface as its correct work. The compiler or interpreter catches only the faults that crash, and the faults left over are the ones that run and return something plausible.

Four kinds recur, and knowing their names helps you look for them. An **off-by-one** error is a boundary mistake of exactly one element. A **swallowed error** is a failure caught and replaced by a default. A **hallucinated API** is a call to a function, method or package that does not exist, or that exists and behaves otherwise. The fourth is not a coding mistake as such, and it is a change that makes the tests pass without fixing the bug. Pearce and colleagues, who generated 1,689 programs from 89 scenarios, found about 40% of them vulnerable, so faults in generated code are not rare.

reveal.text: It returns items 10 to 19. The slice begins at index 10, so the first ten items are never returned.

lead.text: The slice is correct for a caller who counts pages from 0, and it is wrong for one who counts from 1. Nothing in the code says which convention is in use, so the assistant picked one and the caller assumed the other. For page 1 the slice is `items[10:20]`, so the items 0 to 9 are skipped; for page 3 it is `items[30:40]`, which is empty because the list has only 25 items.
The function never crashes, and a casual test of "page 2 returns some items" passes.

lead.text: Here is a billing function an assistant might write: it tries to add up the line items, and if anything goes wrong it returns 0. What it does is turn every failure, whether a None where a price should be or a missing record, into a total of 0, and billing then carries on and issues an invoice for nothing.

The cost of a swallowed error is that the failure is no longer visible. When you read generated code, treat any broad except clause that returns a default as a finding, and ask what the caller does with that default.

reveal.text: It returns 0. The string makes sum raise a TypeError, and the except clause turns that into a total of 0.

lead.text: Ask an assistant to reverse a string and you may get `"abc".reverse()`. Python strings have no `reverse` method, so the call raises an `AttributeError` the first time it runs, which is easy to catch. A fault of this kind announces itself, and tests catch it.

The harder case is a call to a method that *exists* and behaves differently from what the assistant assumed. The list method `extend` adds another list's items in place and returns `None`, so `names = names.extend(more)` throws the list away. The code runs, and the next line fails far from the cause or does not fail at all. Reading generated code means checking that each unfamiliar call exists, and that it returns what the code assumes it returns.

reveal.text: It prints None. sort is a real method, and it returns None because it sorts the list in place.

lead.text: The fourth kind of fault appears when an assistant is told to make a failing test pass. The honest fix changes the logic. A shortcut changes the test, loosening an assertion or deleting the check, or it adds a branch that recognises the failing input, such as returning the expected answer when the year is 1900.

Two habits catch it. Read the test files in the diff before the source files, and be suspicious of any assertion that changed in the same commit as the logic it checks. And search the source for literal values that appear in the tests.

lessons.title: Security review of generated code

blocks.text: A function that looks users up by name, written with an f-string, works for Ana, Ben and every name the author tried. Given the name `x' OR '1'='1`, it does something its author never intended, although nothing in the code looks unusual.
Security faults in generated code are mostly of this kind, familiar patterns that work in ordinary use and fail under a hostile input, so they pass every test written with ordinary input.

intro.promise: By the end you'll spot SQL built from request text and fix it with parameters, find an endpoint that lacks an owner check, and review a new dependency before it is installed.
intro.whyItMatters: Generated code reaches the codebase with the same security faults as the code it learned from.

lead.text: What a model trained on the world's code has learned is what code usually looks like, and a great deal of code in the world is insecure. Pearce and colleagues tested an early Copilot on 89 scenarios chosen for security relevance and found that about 40% of the 1,689 programs it generated were vulnerable. Assistants have improved since, and the underlying difficulty is the same, that the most frequent pattern is not always the safe one.

The prompt asks for a function that finds users by name, and the assistant writes the query by putting the name straight into a string with an f-string. The next screen asks what a hostile name does to it.

reveal.text: All four, because the condition `'1'='1'` is true for every row.

lead.text: With the name Ben the f-string produces `WHERE name = 'Ben'` and one row matches. With the hostile name the quotation marks inside the text close the string early and add a condition of their own, so the query now says `WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'`. The first half matches nobody and the second half matches everybody, so every row is returned.

This is **SQL injection**: attacker-controlled text that alters the structure of a query instead of staying a value inside it. Here it leaks a whole table, and with other text it can change or delete rows.

lead.text: The remedy is not to filter the hostile characters, since lists of bad characters are always incomplete. A **parameterised query** is written with a marker, `WHERE name = ?`, and the value is handed to the database in a separate argument. The database already knows the shape of the query before the value arrives, so the value can only ever be compared, never executed.
When you review generated database code, look for f-strings, concatenation and format calls that build SQL, and ask for parameters instead.
Escaping by hand is a weaker fix than parameters, since it relies on every caller remembering to do it.

reveal.text: None come back. The text is compared as a whole value, and no stored name equals it.
It is authorisation. The endpoint knows who is asking and has not asked whether that person may see this order.

lead.text: **Authentication** asks who you are, and **authorisation** asks what you may do. They are separate checks, and an assistant that writes an endpoint to return `/orders/{id}` will usually add the first and may omit the second. Any logged-in user can then ask for any id, changing a number in the address and reading other people's orders. This is **broken access control**, a request reaching data its caller should not see.

The figure lists four endpoints. All of them require a login. Two of them look a record up by id and return it without comparing its owner with the caller, and those are the faulty ones. The list of the caller's own orders takes the owner from the session, so the caller cannot name someone else, and the delete endpoint checks the owner before acting. When you review, the question for each endpoint that takes an id is whose record this is.

lead.text: Generated code often includes the key it was shown. If it is committed, deleting it in the next commit does not remove it: the earlier commit still holds the file, and anyone who can read the repository can read the key.
The response has two parts. Treat the key as exposed and **rotate** it, meaning issue a new one and revoke the old one, and move secrets out of the source into the environment or a secrets store.

An assistant that needs a library will write an import for one, and sometimes the name is one it has invented. If somebody has registered that name, the install succeeds, and the package may be one an attacker registered because they expected assistants to ask for it. An import that resolves is therefore no evidence that the package is safe. This is **dependency risk**: adding a package that is unmaintained, malicious, or not the one that was meant.

Look the package up before it enters the project. Does it exist in the registry, and is it the one the library's own documentation names? Who maintains it, and does it have a history? When was it first published? A package a few weeks old with one maintainer and a name close to a famous one deserves a closer look than one with years of releases.

recap.keyIdea: Read generated code for SQL built from text, endpoints that take an id without an owner check, secrets in the source and unvetted dependencies, and fix each at the point where it arises.

blocks.text: You saw a single f-string return every row of a table, and a parameterised query return none for the same hostile text. An endpoint that checks the login but not the owner lets one user read another's data, a committed key has to be rotated, and a new package has to be looked up before it is installed.
All of these are claims you can check, and so is anything the assistant says about its own change.

lessons.title: Verifying behaviour

blocks.text: An agent writes a function `my_max`, which should return the largest number in a list, and reports that all tests pass.

The sentence "all tests pass" is something the assistant says, while the log behind it, the code, and the function's behaviour on inputs you choose yourself are things you can see, and they are not equally good grounds for a merge.

intro.promise: By the end you'll total and read a test log, state a property of a function's result, and name the evidence you require before merging.
intro.whyItMatters: An assistant's report tells you what it believes, and the evidence tells you what happened.

lead.text: "I ran the tests and they all pass" is a sentence the assistant wrote. It may describe a real run, and it may describe the run it expected. Nothing in the sentence tells you which, how many tests were counted, or whether the ones that matter were among them. It is a **claim**, and a claim is where verification starts, not where it ends.

Evidence comes in grades, and the figure arranges five of them as a ladder. At the bottom is taking the assistant's word. Above it you can read the code, which shows what the change does and not that it does it. Above that is a test log you have read yourself, then running the feature by hand, and at the top, checking it in a setting that resembles the real one. Each rung rests on more of your own observation than the one below, and the **evidence ladder** is a way of asking which rung a decision is standing on.

steps.headline: Do the tests cover the change

lead.text: Suppose the assistant has written a function `my_max`, which should return the largest number in a list. It starts a running value `m` at 0, and walks through the list, replacing `m` whenever it meets a larger element. The tests it wrote use the lists `[3, 1, 2]` and `[5]`, and both pass.

These two tests contain only positive numbers. You have seen this shape before: an unspoken assumption, here that some element is above 0, that the example inputs happen to satisfy. The next screen asks what the function does when they do not.

reveal.text: It returns 0, because no element is above the starting value and so m never changes.

lead.text: The result 0 is wrong, and the reason is easy to state: it is not in the list. The maximum of a list is one of the list's own elements, whatever the list contains. A statement of this kind, which must be true for *every* input, is called a [[property|A statement that must hold for every input, such as the result being a member of the input. Met in Software Testing and Quality.]], and it is a sharper check than any single example.

You do not need a testing framework to check a property. A loop that generates many small lists, calls the function on each, and asserts that the result is in the list will find the all-negative case within a few tries, and any input that breaks the property is a counterexample you can hand back to the assistant. A second property, that the result is at least as large as every element, would not have found this fault, since 0 is at least as large as every element here, and that is why the first one is worth stating.

lead.text: Once you can tell claims from evidence, you can decide beforehand what evidence a merge needs. This is a **definition of done**, and for assistant-written changes it might read: every criterion in the specification has a test, and you have read the log; no test relevant to the change was skipped; you have run the feature yourself on one realistic input; at least one property of the result has been checked on many inputs; and you have read the diff against the spec.
A rename in a private function needs the log and the diff, and a change to how payments are rounded needs every line.

reveal.text: Nothing. The tests that run the changed module were skipped, so the 64 passes say nothing about the change.

recap.keyIdea: Treat the assistant's report as a claim, read the log and run the change yourself, and state properties that must hold for every input so that one counterexample can overturn a green result.

blocks.text: You read a log by adding its counts and looking at the skipped list, and you found that a function can pass its tests and still return a number that is not in its input. A property states what every result must satisfy, and a definition of done names the evidence you need before merging.
Working well with an assistant also raises questions that are not about correctness at all.

lessons.title: Ownership, licensing and privacy

blocks.text: A customer export of 2,500 rows, each holding a name, an email address and a phone number, is just the kind of file a developer might paste into a chat to ask for a script that parses it. Pasted, it sends thousands of pieces of personal data to a third party.

The mistake is easy to make because a chat window looks like a private conversation, when what it does is transfer data to a vendor under terms that depend on the plan you are on, and the code that comes back may carry a licence of its own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll sort what may be pasted into an assistant, say what to do when a secret has been pasted, and say who answers for the licence of generated code.
intro.whyItMatters: The decision about what to send is made before the assistant sees anything.

lead.text: When you ask an assistant a question, the text of the prompt, the files it reads and anything you paste are sent to the vendor's service, where the model reads them to write a reply. What happens to that text afterwards, how long it is kept in storage and logs and whether it may be used to train later models, is set out in the terms of the plan you are on, and plans from the same vendor can differ.

It follows that a chat is not private simply because it looks like a private conversation, and that the answer to "may I paste this?" depends on the plan as well as on the text. The question that remains for you is what kind of data is in the text.

lead.text: The figure sorts four common cases. A stack trace is usually fine, provided that it holds no personal data; they sometimes do, in an error message that quotes a user's email, so read it before sending. A public README is fine, since the world can already read it. A customer export is not, because it holds personal data about people who never agreed to it being sent to a third party. A production API key is not, because whoever holds the text holds the key.

The last case has a rule of its own. Deleting a message does not recall it: the text has already reached the vendor, and may sit in storage and logs under the plan's retention terms. A secret that has been pasted therefore has to be [[rotated|Replaced with a new one, with the old one revoked. Met in "Security review of generated code".]] straight away. A good habit that follows is to give the assistant the shape of the data and not the data: a few invented rows are enough to write a parser.

reveal.text: Rotate it. The token has already been sent, and deleting the message does not make it useless.

lead.text: An assistant writes code from patterns it learned, and most of the time its output is new in any sense that matters. Occasionally a long block comes out verbatim, or very nearly, from a public project, and that project has a licence. Under a **copyleft** licence such as the GPL, a work that is built on the code and distributed has to carry the same terms, so a verbatim block in a proprietary product can put those terms on it.

Three situations are worth a closer look: a long verbatim block, tests or fixtures copied from another project, and vendored code, meaning a whole library pasted into your repository. In each case the responsibility does not move to the tool that produced the code, and the team that ships the code answers for its licence.

steps.headline: A generated file has 120 lines, and a search finds a distinctive 12-line block in it verbatim in a GPL project. Work out the verbatim share.

workedSteps.text: Count the lines that match and the lines in the file.
The share is the matching lines over all the lines.
Then look at what the block is. A short block that is the core of the function matters far more than its share suggests, so the percentage is where the question starts.

steps.headline: A second generated file has 240 lines, and 18 of them match a project verbatim.

workedSteps.text: The share is the matching lines over all the lines.
The share is wanted to one decimal place.

lead.text: Which tools and plans are approved, given their retention and training terms? Which kinds of data may go into them, and which never? Which repositories may be opened to an agent, and with what access? And what must be checked in generated code before it ships, including a licence check on long blocks and a dependency check on new packages?

Written down as a **team policy**, the answers spare each developer from deciding under pressure, and give reviewers something to point at. Keep the policy short enough to be read, and revise it when a tool's terms change.

reveal.text: A few invented rows. Sending the export would have sent 7,500 pieces of personal data, 2,500 rows with 3 personal columns each, when a parser needed only a handful of invented rows.

recap.keyIdea: Send the assistant only data your policy allows, rotate any secret that has gone into a prompt, and remember that the team that ships generated code answers for its licence.

blocks.text: You sorted four kinds of paste by the kind of data they hold, saw that a pasted secret has to be rotated, and found that a few invented rows serve a parser as well as a real export. Licence risk comes from long verbatim blocks, copied tests and vendored code, and the responsibility stays with the team that ships.
A written policy makes these decisions once.

lessons.title: Working rules and measurement

blocks.text: A team that merged 40 changes a month, with 5% of them failing, merges 60 a month after adopting an assistant, and 10% of those now fail. Counted by merges, that is half as much work again, and counted by failures it looks rather different.
Measuring both how fast changes arrive and how often they fail is how a team finds out whether an assistant is helping, since how a tool feels to use is a poor guide to what it does.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute a change failure rate and read it with throughput, name the cost of skill atrophy, and write a one-page set of working rules.
intro.whyItMatters: Speed is easy to see and quality is easy to lose, so measure both.

lead.text: In the first lesson, experienced developers using AI tools took 19% longer on their tasks while believing they were 20% faster. That gap sets the problem for a team: an assistant feels productive, and a count of merges or lines written is easy to collect and easy to push upward. Neither says whether the work is better.

What matters is what happens to the changes after they merge. Does a change break something that someone then has to fix? How long does it take to restore service when it does? The figure compares two months of one team, before and after it adopted an assistant, with the merges split into good and failed. Switch between the views and look at both bars before reading the next screen.

reveal.text: Good merges rose by about 42%, since the difference is 16 and 16 is about 42% of 38, while failures went from 2 to 6, three times as many.

lead.text: The **change failure rate** is the number of changes that went wrong, divided by the number of changes, as a percentage. The DORA research programme, which studies software delivery, groups its metrics into throughput, meaning how fast changes get through, and stability, meaning whether they work, and the change fail rate is one of the stability measures.

In the merges chart at the start of the lesson the team merged 40 changes before the assistant, at a rate of 5%, and 60 afterwards, at 10%. Multiplying the merges by the rate gives the failed changes in each month, which are 2 and 6, and subtracting gives the good ones.

steps.headline: A second team merged 140 changes in a month at a 5% failure rate. Work out its failed and good merges.

workedSteps.text: The rate is a share of all the merges, so the failed count is the merges times the rate.
The rate applies to all 140 merges in the month.
The good merges are the merges that did not fail.

steps.headline: The next month the same team merged 150 changes at a 6% failure rate.

workedSteps.text: The failed count is the merges times the rate.
The rate applies to all 150 merges in the month.
The good merges are the merges that did not fail.

lead.text: Placed side by side, the two months say two things at once. Good merges rose from 38 to 54, which is 42% more working changes reaching the codebase. Failed changes rose from 2 to 6, which is three times as many. Whether the trade is worth it depends on what a failure costs, and the answer is different for a small internal tool and for a payment system.

A team that watched only merges would see a clear success, and a team that watched only the failure rate would see the rate double from 5% to 10%. Each number is correct and each is incomplete, which is the reason to track throughput and stability together.

reveal.text: 20%. The rate is the failed changes divided by all the changes.

lead.text: A developer who stops writing certain kinds of code, because an assistant always does, gradually loses the fluency to read them critically. The loss is called **skill atrophy**, and it matters here because reviewing generated code depends on exactly the skills the assistant is replacing: you cannot spot an off-by-one in code you could not have written.

The remedy is deliberate, and modest. Choose some work to do by hand each week, particularly the kind of work you will be asked to judge: a function written from a spec before you ask for the assistant's version, a bug traced without help, a diff read before its summary.

reveal.text: Skill atrophy. It is a reason to keep some of this work manual.

lead.text: This course has described a set of habits, and a **working rule** is one of them made short and specific enough to follow. A good set answers three questions. When do I use the assistant? What do I always verify, and how: the diff against the spec, a test log I have read, a property checked on many inputs? And what do I never delegate: perhaps security decisions I cannot explain, work with customer data, or the first draft of anything I am about to be asked to review?
Keep it to a page, put it where you will see it, and revisit it when the numbers say it is not working: a rising change failure rate is a prompt to tighten what you verify.

Throughput and stability belong together, and skills that you stop practising fade, which is the reason to decide in advance what you never delegate.
Across the course the same idea has recurred, that an assistant produces plausible work quickly and that you own what you merge.
