questions.prompt: A tool offers the next few lines of code as grey text while you type, and you press Tab to keep them. Which mode of assistant is this?
hints: The tool reacts to what is under your cursor and nothing else.
It does not open files or answer questions in a conversation.
questions.onCorrect: Completion reads the text around the cursor and writes only what you accept.

misconceptions.feedback: Chat works in a conversation you start, and it replies with text rather than inserting it at the cursor.
An agent opens files and runs commands on its own initiative. This tool only offers text at the cursor.

questions.prompt: An agent edits a function, runs the project's test suite and reports "all 42 tests pass". What does that report establish?
hints: Ask what the 42 tests were written to check.
A report of a run tells you what was run and what happened.
questions.onCorrect: A green run describes the tests that exist, so a change can pass them and still miss what was asked.

misconceptions.feedback: Passing tests show only that the checks that exist did not object. Whether those checks cover the behaviour you wanted is a separate question.
The agent can verify only against the tests it was shown, and those were written before it began and may not describe your request.
The agent ran the suite as written. The limit is what the suite contains, not who selected it.

acceptedIdeas: The 42 tests it ran did not fail on this change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 42 tests it ran did not fail on this change

choices.label: The change is correct, because the tests pass
The agent has verified the behaviour you asked for
The 42 tests it ran did not fail on this change
Nothing, because the agent chose which tests to run

questions.prompt: What is the acceptance rate, as a percentage?
hints: Divide the lines kept unchanged by the lines suggested.
Multiply the result by 100 to get a percentage.
150 lines suggested and 96 kept unchanged: compute 96 / 150.
questions.onCorrect: The rate is 96 kept out of 150 suggested, which is 64 in every hundred.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share rejected. Acceptance counts the lines kept.
That is the count of kept lines. Divide by the lines suggested and express it as a percentage.

questions.prompt: A team's acceptance rate rises from 55% to 70% over a quarter. What does that show?
hints: Look at what the ratio actually counts.
Ask what else could raise the share kept.
questions.onCorrect: Acceptance rate measures behaviour at the keyboard, and quality has to be measured by what happens to the code later.

misconceptions.feedback: The rate counts what people kept. People may keep more because they review less, or because the tasks got easier.
Defects are measured by what happens to the code afterwards, and the acceptance rate says nothing about that.
A higher share kept makes review matter more, because more machine-written lines reach the repository.

acceptedIdeas: Developers keep a larger share of the lines suggested
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Developers keep a larger share of the lines suggested

choices.label: The assistant's suggestions have become more accurate
Reviews of the suggestions have become unnecessary
Developers keep a larger share of the lines suggested
The code reaching the codebase has fewer defects

questions.prompt: An assistant suggests 240 lines across a morning and you keep 180 of them unchanged. What is the acceptance rate, as a percentage?
hints: Use kept unchanged over suggested.
The top is 180 and the bottom is 240.
Compute 180 / 240 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Three quarters of the suggestion was kept as it came.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share you did not keep.

questions.prompt: A tool reads your repository, edits three files and runs the tests. Which mode of assistant is this?
hints: Which mode both changes files and runs commands itself?
Completion and chat do neither on their own.
questions.onCorrect: Reading files, editing them and running commands is what separates an agent from the other two modes.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither completion nor chat edits files or runs commands without you, and this tool does both on its own.

questions.prompt: You are suggested 250 lines. You keep 175 unchanged and keep another 25 after editing them. Counting only lines kept unchanged, what is the acceptance rate, as a percentage?
hints: Lines you edited before keeping were not kept unchanged.
Use the 175 unchanged lines on top and the 250 suggested on the bottom.
Compute 175 / 250 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Edited lines are left out because the measure is about code accepted as it came.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the 25 edited lines as well, but the rate counts only lines kept unchanged.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 175 / 250 = 0.70, which is 70%. The 25 edited lines are not counted as kept unchanged.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the suggestion was not kept unchanged?
hints: The kept share is 65%.
The rest is whatever remains of the whole.
Subtract 65 from 100.
questions.onCorrect: The other 35% was edited or dropped, which is where a reviewer's attention went.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the kept share. The question asks for the rest.

questions.prompt: What share of the codebase fits in the window, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: The share that fits is window divided by codebase.
The codebase needs 600,000 tokens.
Compute 200,000 / 600,000 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: A third of the codebase fits, and the instructions and the conversation use some of that third.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the other way. The question asks what part of the codebase fits in the window.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The codebase needs 600,000 tokens and the window holds 200,000: 200,000 / 600,000 = 0.333, which is 33.3%.

questions.prompt: What share of the codebase fits, as a percentage?
hints: Window over codebase.
The codebase needs 250,000 tokens and the window holds 200,000.
Compute 200,000 / 250,000 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Four fifths fits, so a codebase of this size comes close to fitting but still cannot be loaded whole.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the codebase as a share of the window. Divide the window by the codebase instead.

questions.prompt: An agent has tried four fixes for a failing build. The session now holds the three failed attempts, their error output and your corrections. The fifth attempt repeats an earlier mistake. What is the best next move?
hints: Ask what is taking up space in the context now.
A summary keeps the findings and leaves out the failed attempts.
questions.onCorrect: A fresh session with a summary keeps what was learned and drops the failed attempts that were skewing the output.

misconceptions.feedback: The assistant does not learn within a session. The dead ends sit in the context and pull later attempts towards them.
More text enlarges a context that is already crowded with stale material.
Emphasis does not remove the earlier attempts, which are still in the context.

acceptedIdeas: Start a new session with a short summary of the findings
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Start a new session with a short summary of the findings

choices.label: Ask the same thing again, this time in capital letters
Start a new session with a short summary of the findings
Paste more files so the assistant has more to work from
Keep going, because the history helps the assistant learn

questions.prompt: Which of these is the most useful line in an instruction file?
hints: Ask which line gives the assistant something it could do or avoid doing.
A useful line could be checked afterwards.
questions.onCorrect: A line that names a command can be followed and verified, and a line that names a quality cannot.

misconceptions.feedback: It names no action. The assistant cannot tell what careful would change.
Every assistant already aims at this, so the line changes nothing it would do.
This describes a hope. A line that works names a command, a path or a rule that can be checked.

acceptedIdeas: Run pnpm test before reporting a task done
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Run pnpm test before reporting a task done

choices.label: Run pnpm test before reporting a task done
Follow best practices
Write code that is easy to maintain
Be careful with the database

questions.prompt: A window holds 200,000 tokens. The instruction file takes 3,000, the conversation so far takes 90,000 and the output of commands takes 60,000. How many tokens are left for files you add?
hints: The context holds instructions, history and tool output as well as files.
Add the three amounts already used.
Subtract their total, 153,000, from 200,000.
questions.onCorrect: Less than a quarter of the window is left, which is why long sessions crowd out the files the task needs.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts only the instruction file. The history and command output also occupy the window.

questions.prompt: A codebase has 50,000 lines at about 10 tokens a line. What share of it fits in a 200,000-token window, as a percentage?
hints: First convert lines to tokens.
The codebase is 500,000 tokens.
Divide the window by 500,000 and scale to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Two fifths of the codebase fit, and the instructions and the conversation take part of that share.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the other way round. Take the window as a share of the codebase.
That is 50,000 / 200,000, lines compared with tokens. Convert lines to tokens first.

questions.prompt: Several coding tools read one agreed file name at the root of a repository to find the project's commands and conventions. What is that file called?
hints: The name is plural and ends in the markdown extension.
It is the instruction file for agents.
questions.onCorrect: `AGENTS.md` gives agents one predictable place to look, and some tools also read a file of their own name.

misconceptions.feedback: A README is written for people. The instruction file is read by the assistant at the start of each session and holds what changes its behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which line should be removed from a project instruction file?
hints: Keep a line only if it changes what the assistant does.
Ask what the assistant would do differently after reading each line.
questions.onCorrect: The history of the project changes nothing about how the assistant should edit code, and it takes space on every session.

misconceptions.feedback: It names a convention the assistant can follow and a reviewer can check, so it belongs.
It names a boundary, which is exactly what an instruction file is for.
It names a command and a moment to run it, so it changes what the assistant does.

acceptedIdeas: The project was started in 2019 by a team in Leeds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The project was started in 2019 by a team in Leeds

choices.label: Never edit files under generated/
The project was started in 2019 by a team in Leeds
Use the existing logger module, never print
Run pnpm check before reporting done

questions.prompt: Which of these is a testable acceptance criterion for `slugify`?
hints: A test needs an input and an exact expected result.
Look for the line that a test could pass or fail without anyone interpreting it.
questions.onCorrect: A criterion is testable when it names an input and the result that must follow, so a test can pass or fail it.

misconceptions.feedback: Several different strings could be called a clean, readable slug, so no test could pass or fail this without someone deciding what clean means.
Suitable for a web address is a judgement, and more than one string would satisfy it.
Sensibly leaves the behaviour open, which is the gap an assistant fills with a guess.

choices.label: Given `'C++ & Rust'`, `slugify` produces a clean, readable slug
Given `'C++ & Rust'`, `slugify` produces `'c-rust'`
Given `'C++ & Rust'`, `slugify` produces something suitable for a web address
Given `'C++ & Rust'`, `slugify` handles the symbols sensibly

questions.prompt: What does `slugify('Top  10--Tips')` return under the criteria?
hints: Lowercase first, then collapse each run of spaces or hyphens.
Count each run separately: the spaces after the first word and the hyphens after the 10.
questions.onCorrect: Each run of non-alphanumeric characters, whatever its length, becomes a single hyphen.

misconceptions.feedback: That turns every character of a run into its own hyphen. The criterion gives one hyphen to a whole run, however long it is.
The two hyphens in the input are characters other than letters and digits too, so they form a run of their own and become a single hyphen.

choices.label: `'top--10--tips'`
`'top-10-tips'`
`'top-10--tips'`

questions.prompt: What does `slugify('  Release Notes, v2! ')` return under the criteria?
hints: Look at both ends of the string.
The criterion names the start and the end.
questions.onCorrect: The inner runs each become one hyphen and the runs at the ends are removed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the string before the third criterion is applied, and the criterion forbids a hyphen at either end.
The hyphen at the start has gone, but the criterion applies to both ends.
The hyphen at the end has gone, but the criterion applies to both ends.

acceptedIdeas: `'release-notes-v2'`, with no hyphen at either end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `'release-notes-v2'`, with no hyphen at either end

choices.label: `'-release-notes-v2-'`, with a hyphen at each end
`'release-notes-v2-'`, with a hyphen at the end only
`'-release-notes-v2'`, with a hyphen at the start only
`'release-notes-v2'`, with no hyphen at either end

questions.prompt: Under the four criteria, what does `slugify('  ...  ')` return?
hints: The spaces and dots are all characters other than letters and digits.
Apply the rule about hyphens at the ends last.
questions.onCorrect: This input has no letters or digits at all, which is exactly the kind of edge case an assistant's version is likely to get wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: The one hyphen is right so far, but the third criterion still has to be applied to it.
A dot is neither a letter nor a digit, so the dots belong to the run of other characters and are replaced along with the spaces.
The spaces and dots are all characters other than letters and digits, so they are one run rather than two, and the second criterion gives one hyphen per run.

choices.label: `'--'`, one hyphen for each run of spaces
`'...'`, since the dots are left alone
`'-'`, a single hyphen for the one run of punctuation
An empty string

questions.prompt: An assistant writes this: `def slugify(t): return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", t.lower())`. Run it on four inputs from the criteria: `"  Hello, World! "`, `"A  B--C"`, `""` and `"  ...  "`. How many give a result the criteria forbid?
hints: Work each input through the substitution.
The substitution never trims the ends.
Check which of the four results begins or ends with a hyphen.
questions.onCorrect: The code satisfied the main case and missed the edges, which is the usual pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: The fourth input also fails, since a lone hyphen is not the empty string the criteria require.
The substitution leaves a hyphen wherever a run touches an end of the input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It returns "-hello-world-" for the first and "-" for the fourth, which both break the no-hyphen-at-the-ends criterion. The second gives "a-b-c" and the third "", which are right: 2 failures.

questions.prompt: An assistant writes this: `def slugify(t): return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", t.lower())`. Checked against the four criteria on `"  Hello, World! "`, `"A  B--C"`, `""` and `"  ...  "`, which criterion does it break?
hints: Work out what it returns for `"  Hello, World! "`.
Look at the first and last characters of that result.
questions.onCorrect: It returns `"-hello-world-"` and `"-"`, because nothing trims the ends, and a reviewer holding the criteria finds that in two inputs.

misconceptions.feedback: The function calls `lower()` before anything else, so its output is always lowercase.
The pattern `[^a-z0-9]+` matches a whole run at once, so each run does become a single hyphen.
`re.sub` on an empty string has nothing to replace, so it returns an empty string as the criterion requires.

acceptedIdeas: There is no hyphen at either end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: There is no hyphen at either end

choices.label: The output is lowercase
There is no hyphen at either end
Empty input returns an empty string
Each run of other characters becomes one hyphen

questions.prompt: What do you call an input at a boundary of the usual range, such as an empty string, whose behaviour the spec must state?
hints: The input sits at the border of the normal range.
It is easy to forget because the main case works without it.
questions.onCorrect: An unstated edge case gets whatever the assistant happens to implement.

questions.prompt: Under the four criteria, what does `slugify('Rust 2024: Edition!')` return?
hints: Digits count as alphanumeric characters and stay.
The colon and space form one run and the final exclamation mark is a run at the end.
questions.onCorrect: Digits survive, the inner run becomes one hyphen and the end run is trimmed.

misconceptions.feedback: Digits count as alphanumeric characters, so `2024` stays in the result.
The exclamation mark is a run at the end of the input, and the criteria allow no hyphen there.
The colon and the space after it form a single run, so together they give one hyphen between 2024 and edition.

acceptedIdeas: `'rust-2024-edition'`, with one hyphen between the words
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `'rust-2024-edition'`, with one hyphen between the words

choices.label: `'rust-edition'`, with the digits dropped
`'rust-2024-edition-'`, with a hyphen left at the end
`'rust-2024-edition'`, with one hyphen between the words
`'rust-2024--edition'`, with two hyphens before edition

questions.prompt: A spec says: "`slugify` must not change how article titles are stored." What kind of line is that?
hints: It says what the change must leave alone.
It is neither an input nor a pass or fail result.
questions.onCorrect: A non-goal fences the change in, so the assistant is not free to rewrite storage while it is there.

misconceptions.feedback: An edge case is an input at a boundary, and this line names no input.
A criterion names a result the finished change must show. This line names something it must not touch.

choices.label: An edge case
An acceptance criterion
A non-goal

questions.prompt: `def is_leap(y): return y % 4 == 0` passes tests for 2024 and 2023. Which year would a new test need to use to expose its bug?
hints: Think about years divisible by 4 that are not leap years.
Century years follow an extra rule.
questions.onCorrect: Century years divisible by 100 but not by 400 are not leap years, and the simple test against 4 gets them wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: 2000 is divisible by 400, so it is a leap year, and the function returns the right answer for it.
It is already tested and the function returns False for it correctly.
It is already tested, and the function returns True, which is right.

questions.prompt: A test calls `is_leap(1900)` and stores the result, but nothing compares that result with `False`, so the test passes whatever the function returns. What is the name for the check that this test is missing?
hints: A test with none of these can never fail.
In Python it is written with the keyword assert.
questions.onCorrect: A test that runs code without an assertion adds to coverage and detects nothing.

questions.prompt: What is the mutation score, as a percentage?
hints: The score is faults caught over faults injected.
3 were killed out of 5.
Compute 3 / 5 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Each survivor is an input the tests never checked, so a score of 60% points at two gaps.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that survived. The score counts the faults the tests caught.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three of the five injected faults were caught, and 3 / 5 = 0.6, which is 60%.

questions.prompt: What is the mutation score, as a percentage?
hints: Caught over injected.
The tests caught 20 of 25.
Compute 20 / 25 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Five surviving mutants are five places a defect could sit without a test noticing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that survived. The score counts the faults the tests caught.

questions.prompt: The full rule is: a year is leap if divisible by 4, except century years, which are leap only if divisible by 400. Run the buggy `y % 4 == 0` against the years 1900, 2000, 2023, 2024 and 2100. For which years does it return the wrong answer?
hints: Find the years in the list divisible by 100.
Of those, which are also divisible by 400?
questions.onCorrect: The two wrong years share one cause, a rule the function does not know, so one added test for either one exposes it.

misconceptions.feedback: The list holds another century year that is not divisible by 400. Check each year divisible by 100 against the rule.
2000 is divisible by 400 and so is a leap year, which is what the shortcut says, so the function is right for it.
These are the two test years, and the shortcut classifies both correctly, which is why the tests pass.

choices.label: 1900 only

questions.prompt: 20 faults are injected into a piece of code and the tests catch 15. What is the mutation score, as a percentage?
hints: Caught over injected.
The tests caught 15 faults out of 20.
Compute 15 / 20 and scale it to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The five faults that survived mark the behaviour no test checks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share that survived.
That is the count that survived. The score is a percentage of the faults caught.

questions.prompt: A test calls a function and contains no assertion. What is the effect on line coverage and on defect detection?
hints: Coverage counts lines that ran, whether or not any output was compared.
A test fails only when an assertion does.
questions.onCorrect: Coverage measures execution, and only assertions measure correctness.

misconceptions.feedback: Coverage records which lines ran, and the function ran.
With no assertion the test cannot fail on a wrong result.
Python runs it without complaint. A test with no assert simply cannot fail.

acceptedIdeas: It counts as covered and detects nothing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It counts as covered and detects nothing

choices.label: It counts as covered and detects nothing
It counts as covered and detects every fault
It is invalid and the suite will not run
It counts as uncovered and detects nothing

questions.prompt: What name is given to the share of deliberately injected faults that a test suite detects?
hints: It is a percentage of injected faults that the tests caught.
The faults are called mutants.
questions.onCorrect: A high mutation score shows the suite checks outputs, which line coverage cannot show.

misconceptions.feedback: Coverage is the share of lines that run. The share of injected faults that are detected is a different measure.

questions.prompt: A 900-line change is split into steps of at most 250 lines. What is the smallest number of steps?
hints: Divide the lines by the most lines allowed in a step.
The quotient is not a whole number.
Round it up, because 3 steps of 250 hold only 750 lines.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing gives 3.6, so the count has to be rounded up to 4.

misconceptions.feedback: Three steps of at most 250 hold 750 lines, which leaves 150 lines over.
A step cannot be split, so the count must be a whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 900 / 250 = 3.6, and a step cannot be a fraction, so the smallest whole number is 4.

questions.prompt: A 900-line feature consists of a data query, the formatting of its result, an endpoint that serves it and a screen that shows it. It has to be split into steps of at most 250 lines. Where should the cuts between steps fall?
hints: Think about which pieces could each have a test of their own.
questions.onCorrect: Each seam gives a piece that can be asked for, tested and committed on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: A cut every 250 lines can fall in the middle of a function, which leaves a step that cannot be tested or understood on its own.
An assistant commits in its own working order, which rarely gives a reviewer a unit that can be read and tested alone.
A single 900-line change is the kind a reviewer reads least carefully, which is the reason for splitting it at all.

acceptedIdeas: At the seams between the query, formatting, endpoint and screen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the seams between the query, formatting, endpoint and screen

choices.label: Every 250 lines, wherever that happens to land in the code
At the seams between the query, formatting, endpoint and screen
Nowhere, since one review of the whole change is quicker
Wherever the assistant happens to commit along the way

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number of steps?
hints: Divide 700 by 250.
The quotient is 2.8.
Round up to the next whole number.
questions.onCorrect: Rounding up gives 3 steps, the last of them smaller than the others.

misconceptions.feedback: Two steps of at most 250 hold only 500 lines.
The count of steps must be a whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 700 / 250 = 2.8, which rounds up to 3.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number of steps?
hints: Divide 1,000 by 300.
The quotient is about 3.33.
Round up, because three steps hold only 900 lines.
questions.onCorrect: Three full steps leave 100 lines over, so a fourth is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Three steps of at most 300 hold 900 lines, leaving 100 over.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 / 300 = 3.33, which rounds up to 4.

questions.prompt: After you undo a bad commit, the log still shows the bad commit, followed by a new commit that applies its exact opposite. Which git command produced that history?
hints: The command is named for what it does to the earlier commit.
It adds to the history instead of removing from it.
questions.onCorrect: `git revert` adds a commit that applies the opposite change, so the original stays in the history.

misconceptions.feedback: `git reset` moves the branch back and so rewrites the history. The command that adds a reversing commit has another name.

questions.prompt: A branch holds four commits and the last one is bad. You undo it with `git revert`. How many commits does the branch hold afterwards?
hints: Revert does not remove anything.
It adds one commit.
Four plus one.
questions.onCorrect: The bad commit and its reversal both stay, which is why revert is safe on a branch others have pulled.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count after `git reset`, which removes the commit. Revert keeps it and adds another.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `git revert` adds a new commit that reverses the bad one, so the history grows from 4 to 5.

questions.prompt: A branch holds commits A, B, C and D, and D is bad. Other people have pulled the branch, so you undo D with `git revert`. What does the branch hold afterwards?
hints: Revert does not remove anything from history.
questions.onCorrect: The bad commit and its reversal both stay, which is why revert is safe on a branch others have pulled.

misconceptions.feedback: Removing D from the branch is what `git reset` does. `git revert` leaves D in place and adds a commit after it.
Moving the branch back and keeping the changes staged is what `git reset --soft HEAD~1` does, which rewrites history others already hold.
`git revert` never edits an existing commit. It adds a new one that applies the opposite of D.

acceptedIdeas: A, B, C, D and a new commit that reverses D
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A, B, C, D and a new commit that reverses D

choices.label: A, B and C, with D's changes staged
A, B, C and an edited D with its changes removed
A, B, C, D and a new commit that reverses D
A, B and C

questions.prompt: A 1,400-line change is split into steps of at most 300 lines. What is the smallest number of steps?
hints: Divide the lines by the most lines allowed in a step.
A remainder still needs a step of its own, so round up.
questions.onCorrect: Four steps of 300 hold only 1,200 lines, so the last 200 need a fifth.

misconceptions.feedback: Four steps of 300 lines cover only 1,200.
That is the exact quotient. A step cannot be split, so round up to a whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,400 / 300 = 4.67, which rounds up to 5 steps.

questions.prompt: What name is given to a commit made before a risky step, so that you can return to it?
hints: You make it before the agent starts editing.
It marks the last state you know is good.
questions.onCorrect: A checkpoint costs one commit and gives you a known good state to return to.

questions.prompt: Other people have already pulled a branch that contains a bad commit. Which way of undoing it is safe?
hints: Others hold copies of the existing commits.
Choose the undo that adds to the history.
questions.onCorrect: A revert commit leaves every existing commit in place, so other people's copies still line up.

misconceptions.feedback: A forced push rewrites a history that other people already have, and their copies then disagree with yours.
That destroys the shared history for everyone.
Silent rewriting leaves everyone else with commits that no longer exist on the branch.

choices.label: Rewrite the history without telling anyone
`git revert`
Delete the repository and clone it again
`git reset --hard` followed by a forced push

questions.prompt: A repository holds `app/main.py`, `app/config.py`, `app/db.py`, `app/routes/orders.py` and `tests/test_db.py`. Which file would you open first to see where execution starts?
hints: Execution starts where the application is created and started.
questions.onCorrect: `main.py` usually creates the application and registers the routes, so every request path begins there.

misconceptions.feedback: A configuration module holds settings that other code reads, so it is loaded by something else rather than being where execution begins.
A route module handles one kind of request. Execution starts earlier, where the application is created and the routes are registered.
A test file runs only under the test runner, and it shows what someone chose to check, not where the application itself starts.

choices.label: `app/config.py`
`app/routes/orders.py`
`tests/test_db.py`
`app/main.py`

questions.prompt: The figure shows that `routes/orders.py`, `routes/users.py` and `routes/reports.py` import `db.py`, while `main.py`, `config.py`, `auth.py` and `health.py` do not. How many of the seven other modules do not import `db.py`?
hints: Count all the modules apart from `db.py`.
There are 7, and 3 import `db.py`.
Subtract 3 from 7.
questions.onCorrect: With three route modules reaching the database directly, the data layer is not hidden behind one module.
